title: An-Nur, the Light
hookLine: the Light of the heavens and the earth, light upon light (24:35)

cards: After dark in Medina, long before electricity. In the wall of a house there's a small hollow, a niche, and in it a clay lamp with a wick floating in olive oil. It's the only light in the room.
Faces turn toward it: the edge of the flame, the glow on the wall, the little circle of the world it makes safe. A lamp like that was an ordinary household thing.
And a verse of the Qur'an takes exactly that lamp and makes it a likeness for God's light. Today: An-Nur.

teach.h: THE LIGHT OF THE HEAVENS AND EARTH.
teach.b: Surah 24 is called an-Nur, the Light, and its thirty-fifth verse is the Light Verse. In Pickthall's translation it opens: "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth." Then the picture.
His light is like a niche, and in the niche a lamp. The lamp is in a glass, and the glass is like a shining star.
It's lit from the oil of a blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west, oil so pure it would almost glow on its own, even if no fire touched it. And then two words: "Light upon light."
A niche that gathers the light, a glass that makes it shine, oil that nearly lights itself, a flame: each adds to the one before.
The verse ends by saying God guides to his light whom he wills, and that he strikes these likenesses for people. Commentators have read the picture in many ways.

teach.h: THE HEART, THE PROPHET, THE BOOK.
teach.b: Some say the lamp is the light of guidance in a believer's heart: the chest is the niche, the heart the glass, faith the flame. Some say it's the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, or the Qur'an.
The scholar al-Ghazali built a book around it, the Niche of Lights.
And the Prophet had a du'a asking God to put light in his heart, in his hearing, in his sight, on his right and his left, above and below him, and, in one wording, to make him light.
In that wording, he didn't ask for a lamp. He asked to be one.

how: The Light Verse often appears in calligraphy in mosques and homes, and some Muslims say the Prophet's du'a for light, which a hadith in Sahih Muslim places on his way out to the dawn prayer.

o: the glow of the sun, moon and stars in the sky
a halo shining around a holy person's head
God, whose light is pictured as a lamp in a niche

games.q: what's inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: neither of the east nor of the west

s: commentators all read the lamp the same way
some say the believer's heart, some the Prophet, some the Qur'an.
in the verse, the oil would almost glow even with no fire
so pure it nearly lights itself.
the Prophet asked God to make him light
his du'a asks for light in his heart, hearing, sight and all around him, and in one wording, to be made light.

games.q: the verse describes the olive tree the oil comes from. where does it grow?
o: in the east, where the sun rises.
in the west, where it sets.
neither of the east nor of the west.
games.why: neither of the east nor of the west. some commentators say it catches the sun all day; others read it as beyond any one place.

practice: Sit near a lamp or a window, and let your eyes rest on the light, softly, not staring. Notice the layers: the source, the glass or the shade, the glow it throws on the wall, the light landing on your hands.
Then close your eyes and notice the light is still there, faintly, through your eyelids; if you pray, you can ask God, an-Nur, for light in your heart.

wordCard.voice: An-Nur. The Light: the Light of the heavens and the earth, pictured as a lamp in a niche, light upon light. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: light upon light (24:35). an-Nur, the Light, names the whole surah.

carryVoice: Your line: light upon light. An ordinary clay lamp, holding a likeness of God's light. Day two hundred fifty-five, done.

sources.q: Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth.
